title: We just hit 10,000 downloads on our indie inventory-management game, Backpack Ascendancy! Here’s what we learned building a spatial puzzle RPG for mobile.
author: Great_Ad_615
selftext:
​

Hey everyone! 

​We recently crossed 10,000 downloads on Google Play for our tactical inventory roguelite, Backpack Ascendancy. Looking back at the whole journey, the funniest realization is how wrong we were about where the real difficulty would lie.

​When we started, we assumed the hardest part would be the actual engineering.. getting grid placement, adjacency triggers, custom pixel art, and mobile drag-and-drop to feel snappy on a phone screen. That stuff was definitely a grind, and genuinely fascinating to build.

​Once the core game was running, though, we hit the actual hardest problem in roguelite design: the balancing tightrope.

​Here is what nobody prepares you for until real players get their hands on your game:

​1. Letting players "break" the game (with invisible guardrails)

The entire dopamine loop of a backpack-builder is finding a combination of items that feels completely illegal. You want the player to look at their grid, see an absurd chain reaction of adjacency bonuses, and think, "I just broke the game."

​The catch? If they actually break it effortlessly every single run, the game gets boring in two days. If you nerf everything into the ground so it's strictly "fair," the game feels sterile and frustrating. Designing around that  - running thousands of simulated runs to tweak drop rates and scaling so players feel like they're getting away with murder while we quietly keep the guardrails intact has been the most interesting puzzle I've ever worked on.

​2. Serving two completely different species of players

At 10k players, you quickly realize you aren't balancing for one audience; you're balancing for two extremes at the exact same time:

​The Min-Maxers: Players who immediately dissect every item tag, find three overlapping loopholes we never even considered, and trivialize late-game bosses within 48 hours of a patch.

​The Casual Explorers: Players who jump in on their commute, want to intuitively grasp how items interact without reading a spreadsheet, and hit a brick wall if the early-game onboarding and pacing aren't meticulously guided.

​If you tune the early game for the loophole-hunters, casual players bounce off a brutal difficulty spike. If you oversimplify the mechanics for casual players, the hardcore crowd solves the meta in an afternoon and moves on. Finding a way to make the first ten minutes effortless to grasp while hiding deep, abusable synergies underneath is something we are still constantly refining.

​Hitting 10k downloads as a small indie team has been surreal, mostly because watching real people outsmart our own systems is way more entertaining than building them ever was.

​If you enjoy inventory puzzles, tactical roguelites, or just want to see if you can find a loophole we missed, you can check it out on Google Play : https://play.google.com/store/apps/details?id=com.backpackascendancy.game

Also, interested if any of you has had the same strugfles when building a similar roguelile kind of game. How did you figure out the player progression and ballance ?
